strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Shifting visual anonymization from the input pixel space to the latent representation space of frozen video foundation models (VFMs) is well-motivated, avoiding prohibitive end-to-end retraining while enabling plug-and-play deployment.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method is validated across five distinct downstream tasks (Action Recognition on K400/UCF101/HMDB51, Temporal Action Detection on THUMOS14, and Video Anomaly Detection on UCF-Crime) and across multiple modern video backbones (I3D, VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo).

Effective privacy-utility trade-off: The results demonstrate substantial reduction in private attribute prediction (VISPR cMAP dropped by ~29-35%) with minimal degradation (<1-2%) in primary downstream task performance.

Insightful ablations and bias mitigation study: The ablation studies clearly highlight the crucial role of the latent consistency loss ($L_{LC}$) in preventing catastrophic overfitting to seen proxy tasks, and the experimental evaluation on gender presentation bias on NTU and Toyota Smarthome offers valuable insights into the link between visual privacy and algorithmic fairness.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The core privacy objective (minimizing mutual information between static temporal views via contrastive loss) is largely adapted from existing pixel-space methods such as SPAct (Dave et al., 2022b) and TeD-SPAD (Fioresi et al., 2023). While applying it in latent space with a temporal transformer adapter and an L2 consistency loss is sensible, the conceptual jump is modest.

Limited evaluation against feature reconstruction / inversion attacks: The privacy evaluation is primarily based on linear probe classification on VISPR attributes. In feature-space privacy, an attacker may attempt to invert the latent representations back to images/frames (e.g., via a decoder or GAN inversion). Evaluating defense against feature inversion attacks would significantly strengthen the privacy guarantees.

Clarity regarding multi-task training requirements: In Table 1, it appears the adapter is co-trained on all downstream tasks simultaneously ($\omega_{AR}=\omega_{TAD}=\omega_{AD}=1$). Although Table 4 shows reasonable generalization when trained on single tasks, requiring concurrent co-training on multiple task datasets during anonymization diminishes the claim of being fully task-agnostic.

Stability of the objective: Equation (7) minimizes $\omega_T L_{T^*} - \omega_B L_B$, which involves directly maximizing the NT-Xent loss. Without explicit lower/upper bounds, directly minimizing the negative InfoNCE objective in an unconstrained setting can lead to optimization instabilities or collapsed representations; more details on hyperparameter sensitivity and training dynamics would be helpful.

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: Shifting visual video anonymization from the pixel space (which requires retraining full backbones and is often task-specific) to the latent feature space using a lightweight adapter on frozen video foundation models (VFMs).

Strong empirical performance: Across multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo), SPLAVU achieves a ~30-35% reduction in private attribute prediction on VISPR while maintaining task performance within 1-2% across diverse downstream tasks (Action Recognition, Temporal Action Detection, and Video Anomaly Detection).

Comprehensive evaluation and ablations: The paper provides extensive experiments showing multi-task generalization (generalizing even to unseen downstream tasks without explicit training), ablation of each loss term (validating the necessity of the latent consistency objective), adapter architecture comparisons, dataset scale analysis, and feature precomputation runtime benefits.

Insightful exploration of bias mitigation: Demonstrates that self-supervised latent anonymization helps mitigate perceived gender presentation bias on NTU and Toyota Smarthome without needing explicit demographic attribute labels.
weaknesses: Threat model limitations and lack of feature inversion evaluation: While the authors acknowledge that raw video capture must be trusted, privacy evaluation is limited to attribute classification (linear/MLP probes). Assessing resilience against feature inversion/reconstruction attacks (e.g., training a decoder to reconstruct original frames from the anonymized latent features) would provide a stronger privacy guarantee.

Potential stability concerns with contrastive loss maximization: Maximizing the NT-Xent contrastive loss (Eq. 5) can theoretically cause representations to diverge or collapse without careful balancing against the latent consistency loss. A deeper discussion or theoretical grounding on optimization dynamics and hyperparameter sensitivity of this adversarial objective would strengthen the method section.

Minor notation and typographical issues: In Equation (7), the text immediately following states 'where $\omega_R$, $\omega_T$, and $\omega_B$' while the equation uses $\omega_{LC}$; in Algorithm 1, line 35 incorrectly uses $F_{anomaly}$ instead of $F_{tad}$ for TAD training.

strengths: Practical problem formulation: Moving visual anonymization from input pixels to the latent feature space of frozen video foundation models (VFMs) is practically relevant, computationally efficient, and avoids costly fine-tuning of large backbones.

Extensive multi-task evaluation: Unlike previous methods that evaluate primarily on a single task, this work validates performance across action recognition (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51), temporal action localization (THUMOS14), and anomaly detection (UCF-Crime).

Comprehensive backbones and ablations: The evaluation covers various architectures (I3D, VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo) and provides meaningful ablations demonstrating the impact of the latent consistency objective on generalization to unseen downstream tasks.

Fairness connection: Introducing perceived gender bias evaluation protocols on NTU and Toyota Smarthome provides interesting empirical evidence that spatial attribute suppression can help reduce demographic shortcut learning.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation against stronger privacy adversaries: The privacy defense is primarily evaluated using a linear/2-layer MLP classifier on VISPR attributes. In latent anonymization, a critical threat model involves non-linear adversarial probes or feature inversion attacks (reconstructing raw frames or sensitive facial/demographic features from latent codes). Without testing against feature reconstruction or stronger non-linear attackers, the claimed privacy guarantees remain incomplete.

Conceptual novelty is relatively incremental: The core privacy loss (minimizing mutual information between static clips via an NT-Xent-based contrastive loss) is directly adapted from prior works (SPAct, TeD-SPAD). The technical contribution mainly consists of placing this loss on an adapter module operating on frozen embeddings, combined with a standard L2 feature consistency regularizer.

Inherent tension between latent consistency and privacy preservation: The latent consistency loss (Eq. 6) forces the adapter output to stay close to the frozen features f_E(X), which inherently counteracts the privacy objective of removing static spatial cues. As seen in Table 6, retaining latent consistency severely impairs defense against temporal sensitive attributes like gait (53.45% vs. 26.67% without LC), and in Table 9, higher consistency weights degrade the privacy cMAP.

Minor notations and typos: In Equation (7), the text describes weights '\omega_R, \omega_T, and \omega_B', but the equation uses '\omega_{LC}' instead of '\omega_R'. In Algorithm 1, line 35 erroneously uses 'Fanomaly' instead of 'Ftad' as the input feature set for TAD training.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: Shifting visual privacy preservation from input-pixel modification to the latent feature space is practical, computationally efficient, and well-aligned with the deployment paradigms of modern video foundation models.

Well-motivated and effective loss formulation: Minimizing mutual information between static clips (tiled single frames) effectively removes appearance/demographic shortcuts without requiring sensitive attribute labels, while the latent consistency loss prevents overfitting to proxy utility tasks and preserves generalization to unseen tasks.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across multiple tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, weakly-supervised anomaly detection, video retrieval, gait recognition) and scales across diverse backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, V-JEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G).

Detailed ablations and analyses: The manuscript provides thorough analyses of loss terms, adapter architectures, dataset scaling, unseen task transferability, runtime efficiency, and black-box/white-box inversion attack robustness.

Interesting extension to bias mitigation: Demonstrating that self-supervised appearance anonymization meaningfully reduces gender presentation performance disparities on both synthetic (NTU-Bias) and real-world (Toyota Smarthome) benchmarks is a valuable finding.
weaknesses: Susceptibility to white-box inversion attacks: As shown in Table 8, an attacker with white-box access to the adapter can largely invert the anonymization and recover attribute classification performance close to baseline levels (e.g., 73.7% vs. 76.4% raw on VP-HMDB51). While the authors acknowledge this limitation and note that white-box access may be unrealistic in certain deployment settings, it weakens the theoretical privacy guarantee if the adapter module is distributed publicly or to semi-trusted edge clients.

Potential suppression of useful contextual static cues: Maximizing the distance between static clips forces the adapter to eliminate static spatial information. In fine-grained action recognition or scenes where static contextual background cues are necessary for accurate disambiguation, this could pose a trade-off that is not fully characterized.

Engineering complexity of full multi-task co-training: Concurrently training with heads from distinct architectures (e.g., standard classifier, TriDet for TAD, and MGFN for AD) requires substantial pipeline orchestration. Although Table 5 demonstrates that single-task training with latent consistency generalizes well, clarifying the standard recommended training recipe for practical deployment would be helpful.

strengths: Practical problem formulation: Transitioning privacy preservation from pixel-level frame manipulation (which requires heavy retraining and degrades foundation model representations) to the latent embedding space of frozen video foundation models is computationally efficient and practical for real-world downstream serving.

Comprehensive experimental suite: The paper evaluates across diverse downstream tasks (Action Recognition, Temporal Action Detection, Anomaly Detection, and Retrieval) using multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo), demonstrating that the adapter preserves utility within 1-2% of unconstrained representations.

Well-structured self-supervised objective: Maximizing the NT-Xent contrastive loss between static clips effectively discourages static/spatial attribute leakage while avoiding the need for expensive or incomplete manual privacy annotations.

Thorough ablations: The manuscript thoroughly analyzes adapter architectures (MLP vs. MHSA), loss weightings, data efficiency (training on small datasets like HMDB51), and unseen task generalization via the latent consistency loss.
Exploration of demographic fairness: The paper connects visual latent privacy to mitigating gender presentation bias, introducing targeted evaluation protocols on NTU60 and Toyota Smarthome.
weaknesses: Vulnerability to white-box inversion: Under standard security assumptions (Kerckhoffs's principle), white-box adversaries should be assumed. As shown in Table 8, a gradient-based white-box inversion attack largely recovers the sensitive attribute performance (cMAP increases from 70.5% back to 73.7% on VP-HMDB51), indicating that the sensitive information is linearly suppressed or distorted rather than irrecoverably removed.

Inherent tension in the Latent Consistency Loss ($L_{LC}$): While $L_{LC}$ is crucial for preserving generalization to unseen tasks, it directly penalizes deviations from the raw encoder's feature space ($\|f_E(X) - f_A(f_E(X))\|_2^2$). As shown in Table 7 (gait recognition), retaining latent consistency heavily limits the defense against temporal sensitive attributes (53.45% vs. 26.67% without $L_{LC}$), highlighting an unresolved trade-off.

Ambiguity in reconstruction mitigation claims: In Figure 4 and Section C, the qualitative inability to reconstruct scenes is largely driven by information loss inherent to the global [CLS] token bottleneck rather than the anonymization itself, as demonstrated by the failure of raw [CLS] tokens to reconstruct the input (Figure 4c).

Missing details on multi-task batch scheduling: The training objective (Eq. 4 and Algorithm 1) co-trains on Action Recognition, Temporal Action Detection (TriDet), and Anomaly Detection (MGFN), which operate on very different input structures (trimmed clips vs. untrimmed videos). The paper lacks clarity on the sampling strategy and batch balance used during this joint optimization.

strengths: Pragmatic and timely formulation: Moving visual privacy preservation from input pixel space (which requires retraining full backbones or running expensive generative models) to the latent representation space of frozen video foundation models (VFMs) is practically motivated, efficient, and well-suited for modern large-scale video backbones.

Comprehensive multi-task benchmark evaluation: Unlike prior works restricted to isolated tasks (e.g., action recognition only or anomaly detection only), the framework is evaluated across action recognition (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51), temporal action detection (THUMOS14), and video anomaly detection (UCF-Crime), demonstrating that latent anonymization can maintain cross-task utility.

Strong privacy-utility trade-off: The method reduces sensitive private attribute prediction accuracy (VISPR cMAP down by ~29-35%) while maintaining task performance within 0.2% - 1.5% across various encoders (I3D, VideoMAE-B, V-JEPA, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G).

Thorough ablation and attack analysis: The submission provides extensive experiments analyzing the effect of each loss term, adapter architectures, dataset scale, cross-task generalization on unseen tasks (including retrieval), and resistance against black-box feature inversion attacks.

Exploration of demographic bias mitigation: The paper shows that self-supervised latent anonymization helps reduce spurious correlations and gender presentation bias gaps (evaluated on controlled NTU-60 and real-world Toyota Smarthome setups).
weaknesses: Vulnerability to white-box inversion attacks: As shown in Table 8, under a white-box optimization attack, the attacker recovers an attribute cMAP of 72.6%–73.7% (very close to the raw feature baseline of 75.9%–76.4%). While white-box access is not always guaranteed, open-source adapters and encoders make this a realistic threat model that limits the security guarantees.

Inherent trade-off in the latent consistency objective: The latent consistency loss ($L_{LC}$) forces the adapted features to remain close to the original representations in $\ell_2$ space (weighted heavily at $\omega_{LC} = 100$). While this preserves generalization to unseen tasks, it also retains sensitive temporal/motion signatures (e.g., Table 7 shows gait recognition on Casia-B stays at 53.45% with $L_{LC}$ vs. 26.67% without it). The inherent tension between cross-task utility and temporal privacy deserves deeper discussion.

Ambiguity in adapter input dimensions: In Section 3.2 and Appendix B.1, the paper states that $f_A$ operates on global clip-level embeddings $h_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$, but also describes $f_A$ as a multi-head self-attention module that reasons across the temporal dimension. It is not entirely clear whether $f_A$ processes sequences of temporal clip tokens (e.g., for untrimmed videos in TAD/WSAD) or if self-attention operates over a batch/token sequence in single clips.

Threat model scope: Latent anonymization inherently assumes a trusted extraction pipeline (e.g., on-device camera edge processing before features are transmitted/stored). Raw video frames are still unprotected prior to feature extraction, which limits applicability in setups where untrusted capture devices transmit raw video.
